speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Among others, LTA regulates public transport operators, develops and maintains our road and path networks, regulates vehicles and devices used on our roads and public paths, and enforces against a wide range of transport-related offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA is also faced with a constantly changing transport landscape.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: In particular, the increased use of active mobility in recent years has required LTA to step up its enforcement efforts to strike the right balance between promoting active mobility and ensuring the safety of other users of public paths and roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The first set of amendments enhances our laws to improve active mobility safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Active mobility, which includes walking, cycling and the use of PMDs and personal mobility aids (PMAs), has brought benefits and additional transport options to many Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Some individuals use PMDs to take on food or package delivery jobs, while the elderly and those with walking difficulties use PMAs to get around more easily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The AMA came into force in May this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This laid down the framework of path-sharing rules and regulations, such as where devices can be used and what speed limits they have to adhere to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This was based on the recommendations made by the Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP) in 2016 after extensive public consultation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: There are many responsible device users and cyclists who watch out for other path users, ride at safe speeds, and dismount and push their devices at crowded areas and at traffic junctions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We have also undertaken many efforts to educate and encourage safe riding practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Since February 2018, there have been some 9,000 participants in the Safe Riding Programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Unfortunately, there are still reckless and inconsiderate riders who endanger the safety of others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Much concern has been expressed, including by Members of this House, about the increase in the number of accidents on public paths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Several riders who have caused hurt in accidents have also been charged and sentenced in Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: To further support effective enforcement against reckless behaviour on public paths, I had earlier announced that LTA will be introducing a registration regime for electric scooters (e-scooters) at AMAP’s recommendation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The registration regime will help instil a greater sense of responsibility among owners and users of PMDs, deter reckless riding behaviour and facilitate the identification of errant users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The new Part 3A make registration mandatory for the types of PMDs that the Minister prescribes in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: As recommended by AMAP, we will start with the mandatory registration of e-scooters, which are motorised PMDs with handlebars.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It will be an offence to ride, or to cause or permit to ride, an unregistered e-scooter on public paths, knowing that, or reckless as to whether the e-scooter is unregistered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The applicant will be required to provide his personal particulars which will be stored in a register.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will facilitate the tracing of the person responsible when investigating offences involving a particular e-scooter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The applicant will also be required to declare that his e-scooter is compliant with the width, weight and maximum motorised speed restrictions for PMDs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will ensure that only compliant e-scooters are ridden on our public paths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It will be an offence to make a false declaration during the registration process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Once an e-scooter is registered, the registrant will be issued with a registration mark containing a unique registration number assigned to the e-scooter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The registrant will also be required to make and affix an identification mark, in the form of a sticker, prominently on the e-scooter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Under the new section 20A of the AMA, it will be an offence to ride the e-scooter on public paths without displaying the registration mark or identification sticker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will make e-scooters more easily identifiable to enforcement officers and to the general public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The new section 59A in the AMA also introduces a rebuttable presumption regime for certain active mobility offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is similar to the provisions under the RTA for driver-related traffic offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: If the individual owner of a bicycle, power-assisted bicycle, PMD, motorised wheelchair or mobility scooter fails to provide enforcement officers with information about the rider after a certain offence involving that device has been committed, the owner will be presumed to have been the rider who committed the offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The owner can rebut this presumption by proving that he was not the rider at the time of the offence, such as by showing proof that he was then overseas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This reinforces the duty of owners to ensure the responsible use of their devices, and to assist with the administration of justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill also makes amendments to the regulatory regime for motorised PMAs, that is, motorised wheelchairs and mobility scooters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: PMAs enable the elderly and individuals with walking difficulties to move around.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: In recognition of this need, today’s law imposes fewer restrictions on PMAs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: For example, there are currently no restrictions on the width, weight and device speed for motorised PMAs, and they are allowed to be ridden on pedestrian-only paths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Unfortunately, some people have tried to take advantage of this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Irresponsible retailers have been falsely advertising non-compliant PMDs, such as overweight e-scooters with seats, as mobility scooters to circumvent our PMD regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is despite the fact that these non-compliant PMDs are not designed to meet the usual specifications of mobility scooters, which have seats with back support and substantial footrests as their purpose is to carry individuals who are unable to walk or have walking difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: In addition to irresponsible retailers, some able-bodied users are also using PMAs to circumvent the restrictions on PMDs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will reduce the incentive for able-bodied users to switch to motorised PMAs and safeguard the use of such devices for those who have genuine needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: At the same time, this 10km/h device speed limit will not significantly impact genuine users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Most of the PMAs available today already comply with this speed limit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA will work closely with retailers, hospitals and voluntary welfare organisations to help PMA users adjust to the regulation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: To implement this, the Bill amends section 2 of the AMA to introduce a definition of a "non-compliant mobility vehicle" as a mobility scooter or motorised wheelchair that does not comply with regulations as to the construction of the device.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill also amends the AMA to prohibit the use of non-compliant mobility vehicles on public paths, and to prohibit the sale of such devices by retailers for use on public paths.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This is similar to the treatment of non-compliant PMDs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Apart from improving safety on public paths, we are also concerned about the issue of fire safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: There have been more than 80 fire incidents involving motorised PMDs since 2016.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Currently, many of the motorised PMDs sold in Singapore do not conform to any reliable safety standard.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA has studied the safety standards available today and determined that the Underwriters Laboratories (UL)2272 standard is suitable for application for motorised PMDs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: UL2272 is developed by an independent United States (US) certification company.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Conformity with the standard under UL2272 can significantly improve the safety of motorised PMDs against fire and electrical hazards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Clause 4 of the Bill introduces a new section 19(3) into the AMA to allow the stipulation of such a grace period of usage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: To facilitate the introduction of UL2272 as a technical standard for motorised PMDs, clause 35 introduces a new section 67A into the AMA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This allows LTA to refer to external technical standards without having to reproduce the text of the external material as part of the rule in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: We will then prescribe the requirement for motorised PMDs to comply with the UL2272 standard as a device criterion under the Active Mobility Regulations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Meanwhile, we strongly encourage owners of motorised PMDs to switch to UL2272-compliant devices as soon as possible in order to minimise the fire risk of their devices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: When purchasing PMDs, consumers should try to buy from reputable sources and look out for fire safety standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Consumers should also avoid overcharging batteries, modifying their PMDs or tampering with the electrical components of the PMDs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The second set of amendments will strengthen LTA’s enforcement capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Today, LTA has a team of over 50 Active Mobility Enforcement Officers and cross-trained officers who enforce against errant active mobility users and indiscriminate bicycle parking across the island.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: However, LTA’s active mobility enforcement demands have grown tremendously over the past few years and will continue to rise as active mobility becomes more popular.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: To meet LTA’s increasing enforcement needs, clause 39 introduces new sections 11, 11A and 11B to the LTA Act to allow LTA to appoint outsourced enforcement officers (OEOs) to exercise limited enforcement powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA will be able to contract suitable individuals to exercise limited enforcement powers against selected offences, such as indiscriminate parking of bicycles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Another example is that the OEOs are conferred the power to examine vehicles used on public paths to ensure compliance with the AMA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill demarcates what powers these OEOs can exercise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: In addition, the Chief Executive of LTA will have to explicitly authorise which of the OEOs can exercise which of these powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Chief Executive of LTA will also have the power to specify where and when these OEOs can exercise these powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The Bill expressly prohibits an OEO from exercising any power of arrest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: It also requires them to be in uniform and show their identification cards when exercising their powers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The third group of amendments increases penalties for persons who damage public streets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: There have been several major oil spills and collisions between over-height vehicles and overhead structures, such as pedestrian overhead bridges, in recent years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: These endanger the safety of road users, disrupt traffic, and incur high repair costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: Under the SWA today, it is an offence to cause damage to public streets willfully, but it is not an offence if the action in question is reckless or negligent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: To deter such behaviour, clause 74 of the Bill changes sections 33 and 34 of the SWA in two ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: There is no change to the maximum jail term of six months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA retains the option of suing for the full cost of repair.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The fourth set of amendments facilitates LTA’s efforts to serve notices electronically.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: With advances in technology, many transactions and notifications can now be done via electronic means like email and short message service (SMS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will simplify the notification process and enable faster response by the recipients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: LTA will obtain the person’s consent, whether express or implied, for the use of the electronic mode of service before issuing electronic notices to the person.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: To facilitate this, LTA will also expand the use of its Vehicle Registration and Licensing System (VRLS), which currently allows persons to submit RTA applications and documents electronically to LTA, and allows LTA to serve RTA notices electronically through the system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: The final set of amendments are miscellaneous amendments to update provisions in certain Acts or to bring them in line with other Acts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Lam Pin Min) (for the Minister for Transport)
text: This will provide a better and safer transport landscape for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With easier access to rental bicycles and PMDs that the Minister has spoken about, people are finding it more convenient to move around.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with the Minister that many users are responsible.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we, too, know of incidents whereby pedestrians were knocked down by cyclists or PMD users who were reckless, or fires which occurred due to overheating of batteries while these devices were being charged.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important for device owners and users to exercise greater responsibility and ensure the safety of others beyond the convenience of themselves.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, beyond the recommendations made by AMAP, such as reducing speed limits or wearing of helmets by cyclists, I have four suggestions to make.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The challenge is how to best redesign existing lanes or add on new ones to accommodate all types of users.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It also includes erecting more signages and clearer warning signs where it is either prohibited to use certain devices or where restrictions exist.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that, soon, more such improvements will be made across the Island.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, I hope MOT can implement more Silver Zones in more older estates sooner.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With better designed roads and pavements, more traffic-calming features, clearer signages, one part of the equation to have a safer and more pleasant commute for everybody will be in place.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: PMD users, especially frequent daily users, such as those who use it to deliver food, couriers, should take out such insurance.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, many households are likely to be cycling or using PMDs only on a recreational basis, or infrequently.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, to make such insurance plans more affordable and flexible may be the way to go.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I hope that AMAP can work with the insurance companies to design more flexible insurance packages and coverage so that more users, whether the regular users who use them for their work or the recreational users who use them for the family, can find it easier to buy such insurance.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will be particularly important for users to be insured so that, if there is an unfortunate incident of accident, the coverage can allow claims to be made from the insurance.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thirdly, earlier we heard about enforcement against errant users and retailers.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Accidents involving PMD users or bike-cyclists sometimes can involve minor injuries, at times serious injuries, and even deaths.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: LTA has been issuing advisories and summonses to many cyclists and PMD users for unsafe riding.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I want to commend them for their greater and more visible enforcement actions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has helped to highlight the importance of having people who obey and have proper riding behaviour, rather than those who are errant in their behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, we also hear of efforts against errant retailers of PMDs and Power Assisted Bicycles (PABs) who are not compliant.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such operations by LTA and the Traffic Police are important and should be encouraged.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, I would like to call upon LTA to offer a listing of more than just reputable sources of retailers – a listing to which all users can go through, knowing that any items that are sold will be those that are compliant.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, beyond reputable sources, I hope the Senior Minister of State can work with MOT or LTA to give a listing to assure all consumers that any devices that they purchase in Singapore will be compliant.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will enable our users to have peace of mind knowing that they have bought from retailers in Singapore who have complied with all the rules and regulations.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This programme can work closely with the Traffic Police who similarly have other related programmes.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If both agencies can partner and pool their resources together, I am quite sure the 9,000 or more users or commuters who will learn and benefit from such safe riding programmes will be multiple-fold in a shorter time period.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, beyond legislation and enforcement measures, what is of utmost importance is for every pedestrian, driver or PMD user to be more considerate to other users while adhering to the rules and regulations of our roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The irony of what this elderly man had said was not lost on me at all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope it will encourage all owners to adopt a more responsible and safe usage of their PMDs, though the extent to it remains to be seen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I read from the Explanatory Statement to the Bill that if the registration of a registrable PMD or PAB has been cancelled, the person last registered will be treated as the owner.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This seems to differ from vehicle registration and it seems to be at odds with property law principles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the previous registered owner sells the PMD to another person, who registered it under his name, but for some reason, the registration was cancelled, it would be odd and illogical for the previous owner to be regarded as the owner again by virtue of this law alone.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He would have been paid a fair price by the new owner or buyer.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may also not be fair if such previous owner has to bear any legal consequences arising from the use of the PMD which has nothing to do with him.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, assuming that a person has sold his PMD to another person, can the owner deregister himself unilaterally and after that legally, he would have nothing to do with what the new owner does with the PMD?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or does the owner have to make sure that the new owner registers himself?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That would not seem to be practicable again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, this Bill seems to have put the presumptive onus and burden of proof on owners in respect of their devices' technical compliance with the requirements of the law.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, are there any agencies or appointed operators or even fact-checking websites or apps which owners can approach to seek verification of technical compliance of their devices prior to purchase?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill does not consider providing an age restriction to the use of PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does or will the underaged offender receive the same punishment as an adult offender?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill makes it an offence under the RTA to drive a motorised wheelchair or mobility scooter on the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the illegal use of PMDs on roads may have grabbed all the media attention, the use of motorised wheelchair or mobility scooters on roads is not an infrequent occurrence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the COS debates in 2016, I said in my MOT cut, and I quote, "for the suggested ban on use of PMAs on roads to work effectively and reasonably, there must be user-friendly pavements on every road, otherwise, such a ban will not be practical or fair." PMAs were previously the preferred legislative synonyms for motorised wheelchairs or mobility scooters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two years down the road, I still see motorised wheelchairs or mobility scooters on the roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Near where I live, there is an elderly uncle who often rides his mobility scooter on the roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He rides ever so slowly along the road as I wait patiently behind him in my car or sliding to the left to let him pass by.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I feel so stressed for him, while he rides by calmly and oblivious to the risks which I see.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I agree that motorised wheelchairs or mobility scooters should not be allowed on roads for safety reasons, I am quite concerned that, many times, such users may be forced to use the roads because of the lack of access or constraints in access on supposed pavements or footpaths along the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also take care that when there are roadworks or curb-side works, access must not be limited or be blocked at all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will contractors be required by authorities to provide alternative off-road access for motorised wheelchairs or mobility scooters?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask the Government that in the case where a motorised wheelchair or mobility scooter user can prove that he was forced to access a road because the pavement or footpath has been obstructed in any way, will that be a complete defence and will he be let off?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And finally, what are the authorities' efforts to ensure that access on footpath or pavement remains unobstructed?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This proposal has received much negative response from cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a cyclist, I can understand why cyclists feel that 10 km/h may be too slow for many cyclists.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But let us not also forget that until recently, the law did not even allow bicycles on footpaths but for the fact that this law was never adequately enforced, just as we still often see many cyclists continue to cycle against the traffic or beating the red light.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The recent change in law allowing bicycles on footpaths also coincided with the proliferation of PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The poor cycling culture coupled with the lack of enforcement by authorities over the years meant that we need to create from scratch a new culture of safe and considerate use of bicycles and PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has proven to be a huge challenge.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to engender this culture not just amongst cyclists and PMD users, but also pedestrians and other footpath users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, how do we get people walking on footpaths or connectors to keep left or keep a proper lookout for other users?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are we doing enough to educate everyone and not just cyclists and PMD users?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: AMA allows different usage of different paths by different types of bicycles or mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, how many people are actually aware of the restrictions for each type of bicycles and mobility devices, and who and what is allowed on which paths?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not just referring to cyclists or mobility device owners.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Walk around a Housing and Development Board (HDB) estate or a public park, and try asking residents or park users what are the new rules under the AMA, and who and what are allowed on which paths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not be surprised to find out that many still do not know the answers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When new rules requiring members of the public to make changes to their behaviour in public, authorities have to make sure that information reach members of the public and, indeed, different types of path users through various means.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should never just be assumed that people must be taken to know the rule change without ensuring that the communication had been successfully done.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More than half a year ago, a park connector near my home had its lines redrawn between Kembangan Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station and the East Coast Parkway by Marine Terrace.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most parts of the park connector had a line drawn across one-third of the path.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At certain intervals along the connector, on the narrow side, there is a diagramme of a person walking, painted in yellow on the path.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The wider side of the path is marked with the initials "PCN".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before these new lines and markings were added, most people and cyclists kept left when heading one way or the other along the connector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the redrawing of lines, some who walk along the connector try to stay on the narrower part of the connector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this part is really narrow and cannot accommodate more than two persons walking abreast.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The keep left practice seems to have been abandoned by many and there is often a spillover to the PCN part when people walked past one another in the opposite direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Meanwhile, many continue to walk on the PCN part, including some with their pet dogs or strollers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Cyclists and PMD users are left wading through the traffic on both sides of the line, frequently unsafely, and not always through any fault of their own, depending on the traffic flow of those walking or jogging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what is actually the appropriate way for the different users to use the park connector with the lines drawn in this way?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To makes things worse or more confusing, between 20 metres (m) and 100 m before a road crossing, the lines and the markings completely disappear.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what are people supposed to do when the markings disappear?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Pretend that there are an invisible line and similar markings?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a change is expected for such a short distance, it can be pretty chaotic, too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More importantly, how do the authorities educate the public and ensure that people get used to using such paths according to the law and in a safe and predictable manner?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the lines and markings were first painted, I have been looking out for advisories to the public placed along the connector.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Adopting an attitude of ignorance of the law may not be an excuse, it is not going to make things better and safer for all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those in charge will only be kidding themselves if they do.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I filed the PQ after some cyclists wrote to me, citing that many are still unaware of the rule change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Participants in the Safe Riding Programme developed by LTA and the Singapore Road Safety Council are also informed of this width limit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It sounds good, but has enough been done?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why are people still surprised to hear the rule change and, worse still, had their bicycles confiscated without knowing the rule change?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides the cyclists and mobility device owners who must know the changes in law, the pedestrians and other users of footpaths must also know.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will, in turn, enable everyone to assert their rights, promote mutual respect and consideration among different users and, hopefully, in the process, with time, bring about this change in culture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government will consider enhancing its efforts in public education beyond its current efforts to reach out to cyclists and PMD users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, we are back here again with yet more amendments to existing statutes mostly relating to the regulation of PMDs and bicycles as well as shared use of footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, as PMDs become more popular, there have been more news about accidents involving errant riders on roads and footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What he meant was, in the earlier years, bicycle owners must register their bicycles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps some of us may still remember what the licence plates look like.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have spoken before in Parliament that creating a safe riding culture for PMD users and cyclists is very important.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also mentioned that we should do it through two methods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first is through consistent enforcement of the law, and the second is through adequate public education.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To encourage citizens to abide by the law, enforcement must be as consistent as possible so that people understand that they will not get away easily with any infraction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because we currently have different regulations targeting the different types of PMDs and bicycles, it is important to educate the various types of device users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if riders are unwilling or not required to attend these courses, can they still receive the safe-riding messages?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides targeting riders, public education should also target pedestrians and footpath users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our public education must be extensive, so that regardless of age, race and culture, all will have access and not just be limited to those who wish to know about these messages.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But how many people actually know what are the requirements prescribed by the law, for example, what devices are allowed to be used on which surfaces, what are the speed limits?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides online information on the requirements of active mobility statutes, are such information given out at exhibitions and courses alone?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is such information given out in hardcopies to every household?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is such literature in Chinese, Malay and Tamil, in addition to being in English?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I feel that there is still much for us to do to achieve a safe riding culture where there is a culture of safe and considerate use of PMDs and bicycles.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is, indeed, regrettable that in our effort to improve the mobility of residents and encourage people to enjoy the outdoors without relying on the use of traditional transport like motor cars and other petrol or diesel vehicles, we are, today, confronted with another set of problems.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The issues that confront us are clearly placed into two categories.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, it is the lack of civic mindedness on the part of those who use these new generation mobility devices; and second, it is the lack of strategic and forward planning on the part of the transport authorities in allowing the owners of these PMDs free reign on public pathways and pedestrian walkways.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I feel compelled to say this of the authorities as I read the Bill which states "Registration of registrable personal mobility devices – purpose of Part 528A".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The purpose of this Part is to provide for the registration of PMDs to enable the use of PMDs on public paths to be regulated for reasons of safety and law enforcement.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Yes, we should have thought of safety long before these 20-40 kilogramme (kg) missiles go crashing into innocent pedestrians.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, we are constantly playing catch-up, though I would say it is better than turning a blind eye or a deaf ear to the public outcry for protection against those who use their PMD recklessly.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents told me that it is no longer safe to walk in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They say that they can be knocked down by PMDs, bicycles anytime, anywhere.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are we too hasty to be car-lite when the mindset of our people and the infrastructure are not ready?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The AMA seems to favour cyclists and PMD users.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At areas where there are high pedestrian traffic and narrow passageway, I am sure Members will agree with me that it is near impossible to have both cyclists and pedestrians to co-exist.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, in Nee Soon South, we put up "Dismount and Push" or "No Cycling" signages, and this is to remind cyclists to refrain from cycling through these narrow passages.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: From time to time, there is joint enforcement action by the Police and Town Council, and this is to ensure the safety of our residents in common spaces.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, one resident challenged our enforcement action when he was issued with a ticket.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He said he worked in LTA and he is in the Active Mobility Team, and he knows that all these "No Cycling" signages are no longer legal, no longer applicable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In short, what the Town Council is doing is "Tak Pa Kai".

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: My question is: does this Active Mobility Team member like him understand the ground?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Does he care about the need on the ground?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Or is he more interested to push through the Act and encourage cycling at all costs?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope my favourite Minister can review the Act and put in place more equitable law for public safety.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I ask this because the victims cannot seek any compensation for medical treatment and the continued expenses that would be incurred in looking after someone who becomes an invalid, or to be compensated for loss of a loved one.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another area we need to look into is the need to take enforcement action against shops or anyone selling these PMDs which do not comply with the new regulations or which perform illegal modifications on these devices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Strong enforcement action must be done to swoop down on these outlets, some of which may still be holding stocks of devices which do not comply with the law, and some operate out of HDB flats.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another area that I want to raise is what about those who use their handphones when they are riding on their PMDs?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen on several occasions riders looking at their handphones while they cruised down the pathways.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is another reckless behaviour that can result in an accident.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to point out that there are elderly people on their motorised wheelchair whom I have seen watching video clips while riding on pathways.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Again, this must be put to a stop.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Should a pillion rider be allowed on PMD at all?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The weight of one or more persons may undermine the effectiveness of the PMD braking system.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Quite often, I see very young kids, barely six to eight years old, riding pillion on PMDs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And it is also timely to remind all PMD users, as well as drivers of motor vehicles that they should observe the traffic rules and take precaution when on the road, at traffic light junctions or near pedestrian crossings.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They should not take for granted that the other party knows or will do what you think they would do to give way, or to have right of way.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Road safety and precaution must be practised by everyone.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Another question I would like to raise is whether there will be an age limit to allow a person to register a PMD.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the case of a driver’s licence, anyone aged 65 and above needs to go for a medical check-up to get a licence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will this apply to those using PMDs in the interest of the public?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, it may be important for the riders to be sure they are able to manage their PMD or motorised wheelchair for their own safety, especially if they have weak eyesight, or are on medication which can impair their judgement or cause drowsiness.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The rider rode the PMD down a flight of staircase and injured himself.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When he was sent to hospital, it was found that actually he has dementia.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to ask, under section 28D, the authority may cancel the registration of a registrable PMD if (a) the authority is satisfied that the PMD: (a) has ceased to be used on any footpath or shared path in Singapore; (b) has become wholly unfit for further use.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how will the authorities determine if a device has ceased to be used on any footpath?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is it the onus of the owner to declare that he does not intend to use it outside his house and so he can sort of "hang up" his PMD?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Afterall, the device is not subject to any annual inspection.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):	It is said that better late than never.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am pleased that, finally, we will have laws to regulate these PMDs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, we need stiffer laws in several areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If the pillion rider is a child, the child's life could also be endangered.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our laws can take these into consideration.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Earlier, it seemed that we had rushed to allow these PMDs on roads without considering that our infrastructure is not yet ready, and this has posed dangers to pedestrians.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even the current Bill has areas that are not covered.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can amend as soon as possible to keep our pedestrians safe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This is a positive sign, I believe, of the Government’s commitment to being responsive to the evolving challenges in this new area of land transport management.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Since the AMA was passed last year, the challenges associated with the regulation of the use of bicycles and PMDs have become even more noticeable, sharpening public debate on both sides.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is very difficult not to encounter such devices in public spaces, regardless of whether one is travelling as a pedestrian, a driver or a public transport user.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This brings up the question of whether the impact of the use of such devices, as well as bicycles, PABs and PMDs, on the majority of road users has been a positive or negative one, and whether the way we manage the use of these so-called transport alternatives is on a sustainable path.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There is little arguing that the movement to encourage active mobility has tremendous potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And it is a worthwhile attempt to work towards the ultimate goal to promote more effective last-mile connectivity and reduce our heavy dependence on private car usage as a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the best of intentions, however, Sir, one of the most intractable problems we face as a nation with a heavy dependence on cars is not the cars themselves, but the negative habits associated with heavy car usage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: These habits are familiar ones – indiscriminate parking, a lack of consideration for other road users, a refusal to adhere to rules and regulations about road use, dangerous driving, a refusal to give way, and the list goes on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: These habits are not caused by the cars themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I have no doubt that they can just as easily, if not already, become grafted onto any forms of transport alternative, and the problems will not only persist, but grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My understanding, Sir, is that PMDs and similar devices are meant to promote last-mile connectivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But it seems clear that a lot of the issues that we see arise are precisely because some users choose these devices as their main and preferred mode of transport.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Given our space constraints, the rise of PMDs and similar devices as the primary mode for making a full journey from point to point means that they have become the alternative to what had earlier been the main modes of transport.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This convenience to these individuals comes at a cost to other road users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even with the enforcement updates contained in this Bill, it is not clear if they will be up to addressing the increasingly complex challenges associated with changing usage patterns of PMDs and similar devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is not difficult to observe these changes, and some of them cause tremendous concern.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At any time during the night at various parts of the island, it is now not uncommon to observe groups of riders, many of them young, gathering in their helmets and e-scooters, often smoking with their electronic devices ever-ready, decked out for what appears to be long journeys in convoys that stretch and proceed at speeds that would be uncomfortably high to any pedestrian out for a night stroll.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Even if these large groups of users were mostly confined to footpaths, it is hard for drivers not to notice them when they go against the flow of traffic, because of the glare of their bright headlights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these groups seem to be quite uncompromising in their lack of desire to give way, as many reported incidents already show.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There is another phenomenon that I had already noticed and which I asked the hon Minister for Transport about in an earlier PQ at a previous Sitting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And this is a habit which appears to be becoming increasingly prevalent and which the hon Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah earlier alluded to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Who will be responsible if children being ferried as pillion riders are hurt when a rider misjudges the stopping distance of his extra load, for instance?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I would like to urge the Ministry to continue to look into these enforcement issues early and to ensure a framework that all users can benefit from in a manageable, yet cost-effective way for enforcement becomes available early on.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In particular, I welcome the greater regulation in the use of PMDs in Singapore in a manner that will ultimately benefit both commuters and pedestrians where safety is concerned.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These accidents, even if it is not fatal, can still result in serious injury, as I have seen in PMD accidents that happened in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One fatal or serious accident would be one accident too many.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An accident is an experience that would be very traumatising for those involved, but further issues like compensation and civil lawsuits can further complicate the situation.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Already in Japan, Osaka City and Nagoya City require bicycle riders to have liability insurance as a condition for riding in the city.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe this issue of having PMD users to have a liability insurance should be studied, and we could model after Japan's practice, considering Japan is far ahead in possessing a "riding culture" amongst its many commuters.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, accidents involving PMD users can still result in serious injuries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Accidentally brushing against a car can incur thousands of dollars in compensation for repair costs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the younger profile of several PMD users in Singapore, an attempt to recoup thousands of dollars in damages would pose a heavy financial burden for both victim and accused, not to mention the costs involved in pursuing recourse, such as civil lawsuits.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, mandating personal liability insurance would not only provide better liability coverage for PMD users, but victims of accidents are able to seek proper recourse to claim their damages.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Using a PMD in the presence of other pedestrians entails certain responsibilities, and I strongly believe that having a personal liability insurance is one of them.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would go further to suggest leveraging technology to notify users of the need to renew their insurance together with their PMD registrations annually, if such liability insurance is made mandatory.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Insurance companies can tier their premium for such liability insurance depending on the risks involved in insuring different age groups.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):  : I support the LTEM Bill, particularly amendments that will be made to AMA.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to urge the Government to take the opportunity from this amendment to mandate the purchase of personal accident insurance coverage for users of PMDs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is important to ensure that those who are involved in PMD accidents, particularly pedestrians, can make the necessary compensation claims for their injuries.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The purchase of personal accident insurance for the usage of PMDs was introduced in several cities in Japan, and we can learn from their experience in this issue to create a safer environment for both PMD users and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): PMDs may be a key feature in our active mobility landscape and I do not deny their value in providing alternative commuting methods for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, as with the introduction of all new cultures that come with technological advancement, proper care must be taken so that we can have greater peace of mind for all Singaporeans that share the same space.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore may be small, but I dare say we are not so small that we cannot cultivate a proper, responsible riding culture here as well, like those that are found in other countries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mobility vehicles are sustainable alternatives that have evolved to meet the transport needs of an urban environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When used responsibly and safely, they provide greater convenience, promote public transportation by providing first- and last-mile connections, and are themselves a form of recreation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How the different users navigate and share public spaces in land-scarce Singapore can be a significant source of friction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mobility vehicles are perceived as competing with pedestrians for space and posing threats to pedestrian safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My residents regularly provide feedback about these dangers and want the Government to do more to protect residents and pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My residents also regularly see me when they get fined and say the Government is enforcing too much and needs to relax a bit when it comes to mobility vehicles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Gavin Chan highlighted to me on Facebook, we should think about longer-term social norms we want to inculcate for public path and road use, whilst addressing short-term pain points through legislative reforms and refinements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This should be done with the participation of all users.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To this end, I note and welcome the incremental, consultative and education-based approach the Government is taking in its regulation of mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of these amendments are based on observations from the implementation of AMA, which came into effect this year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The AMA Panel has also been very active, just recently releasing their second recommendation report.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be possible, for instance, for a food delivery company to own a fleet of PMDs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, can the Minister clarify whether there is an obligation on the registered responsible person to update the register upon a change of ownership or when the PMD ceases to be used?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can the authority refuse registration of a PMD on the basis that the applicant had previously been convicted of mobility vehicle-related offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also understand that the obligations of an owner of a PMD or PAB continue even after cancelling their registration, as the person last registered will be treated as the owner under the definition of "owner" if the registration has been cancelled.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can owners safeguard themselves against continuing liability for offences relating to a PMD or PAB, even after cancelling their registration?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether enforcement powers exercised by these outsourced enforcement officers, public path wardens and volunteer path wardens are public powers that would be similarly amenable to judicial review?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the rationale for removing this requirement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Has this requirement been proven to be too onerous for LTA?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the new registration requirement for PMDs, it would surely be easier to locate the owner for this class of mobility vehicles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, the reasonable inquiry requirement might have provided a counterbalance to the expansion of the power of disposal now conferred on outsourced enforcement officers under the new section 50 of AMA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, clause 3 amends section 18 of AMA, which includes the use of PMDs on footpaths.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last year, Minister Khaw Boon Wan responded to a PQ stating that footpaths in Singapore are wide enough to accommodate both pedestrians and cyclists at the same time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He stated that most of the country's footpaths are at least 1.5 metres wide, while footpaths near town centres and MRT stations are generally wider, between 2.4 metres and 3.6 metres.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In his response, Minister Khaw considered that such width is sufficient to accommodate both pedestrians and cyclists.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can the Minister provide an update on any works it has undertaken to widen footpaths that might be too narrow to safely accommodate both pedestrians and mobility vehicles?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These four areas are critical to help reduce the incidence of accidents involving PMDs, PABs, mobility vehicles and motorised wheelchairs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, the amendments are in line with the overall goal of encouraging more Singaporeans to adopt an active lifestyle by encouraging more alternative forms of transport in their daily commute.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On the amendments in section 41, clause 20, sufficient information ought to be circulated to the public to inform them of the conferment of powers on outsourced enforcement officers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that the public know and recognise the authority given to Active Mobility Patrol (AMP) and Public Path Wardens (PPW) to facilitate law enforcement.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: One of the difficulties faced by such volunteers was convincing people of their authority despite having LTA cards.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Quite a handful of cyclists and riders of PMDs do not believe that the AMP volunteers have the power to stop them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Recognising such authority is pivotal for the officers to carry out their jobs without fear and prejudice.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, information on how to recognise and distinguish between what is classified as a PMD, PAB or motorised wheelchair should be stepped up, to encourage awareness among the public on what is allowed for acceptable use.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Sellers, too, need to be educated and are required to provide and display such information in a reasonably visible manner when one purchases such devices.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, we should look at the demographics of the individuals that were involved in accidents and then peg the pseudo legal age.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should also note that the requirement for critical judgement when riding the PMDs is no less than that required of a driver.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, we also must take special care to ensure that these new regulations do not affect users of PABs and motorised wheelchairs, which rely on these vehicles as their primary mobility aid.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of banning it altogether, we can consider a system where PMDs can be used on footpath during off-peak hours where human traffic flow is minimal, to minimise disruption to users with legitimate needs and uses.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To put things in perspective, instead of giving a summons when one has erred, an incentive-based system could be the situation where upon registration of the mobility vehicle, a lump sum disguised as tax is collected.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Upon end of every work year, should the individual not err, the lump sum will be returned to that individual.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, this may invoke a healthier habit of keeping safe and conforming to the rules, rather than people trying to evade punishments.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have witnessed some of these riders myself, speeding on their e-scooters on the road without consideration for other road users and motorists, risking their own lives and the safety of others.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should complement and augment the efforts of our manpower resources with technology aids, such as street cameras, other high-tech devices and artificial intelligence (AI) to deter reckless users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides speeding and inconsiderate riding, some riders actually break the law by using unauthorised PMDs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the common reasons given by such users who were caught was that they had always presumed that it was the sellers’ responsibility to ensure compliance of the devices with LTA’s regulations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does this mean that the Government intends to inspect all models available in the Singapore market?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Moving forward, we have to reach out to PMD users and potential users to educate them on considerate and safe riding, how to do so, the new regulations, and the consequences of violating the law, including the impact on those they injure or kill, the fines and potential civil liabilities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They should also learn from where and how to buy approved PMDs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry share with us what other public educational measures will be implemented to reach out to all individuals and households?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin): In the past few years, accidents caused by reckless riders of PMDs have been increasing.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have personally seen on several occasions youngsters riding e-scooters recklessly, posing risks to road users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My residents have also given me feedback about this.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The new regulations that this Bill will implement will help improve the current situation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since enforcement work is very labour-intensive, I suggest that the Government adopt more high-tech auxiliary equipment, including AI, to improve the efficiency of supervision.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To make our shared paths safer, it is not a one-night process.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government can launch more public education programmes to teach riders how to use PMDs on shared paths safely and politely.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They will allow LTA to outsource enforcement to boost the team of officers and ensure compliance with AMA.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We will need more enforcement officers in order to have sufficient deterrent effect against errant PMD users and cyclists.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So far, the enforcement has been a bit of a hit-and-miss.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not easy to catch errant ones as there are so many users and they are everywhere, even riding their devices along common corridors and void decks of our HDB blocks, shopping malls, hawker centres and even community centres and MRT stations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my constituency, we have many elderly residents who have been complaining to me about all the near-misses they have experienced.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Near the Bukit Merah View Market and Food Centre, there is a short cut to access a housing estate and many PMD users zip around and through the food centre.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The situation is so bad that even the stallholders complain to me.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the e-scooter users are advised not to use them in the market, some of them become aggressive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There is a palpable sense of entitlement and, to them, pedestrians are obstacles which should move out of the way at the sound of their bells, if they bother to ring them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is unfortunate that residents no longer feel safe on shared paths.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Gone are the days of leisurely walks on park connectors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One has to be perpetually on the lookout and “look-over”, that is, look over your shoulder if you do not want to be knocked down.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My seniors tell me that they feel tense when they go on walks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They feel even more tense when they bring their grandchildren out.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are aware that their eyesight and hearing are no longer as good and their reactions are slower.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They worry about their ability to protect the young ones in the prams and keep active toddlers out of the way of cyclists and e-scooter riders who can appear very suddenly.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some senior citizens ask me why the Government is promoting the use of PMDs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Allowing the proliferation of PMDs seems to go against our current drive to promote a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of us will remember the National Steps Challenge, which encourages the average Singaporean to walk 10,000 steps a day.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Even for non-PMD users, reaching 5,000 steps is already quite difficult to achieve.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For PMD users, the number of steps would definitely be far lower.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I ask the Government to reconsider our stand on the use of PMDs in the context of national health and the potential disease burden.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the past two years, the accidents caused by the black sheep amongst them have caused many people to be seriously injured and even unconscious, making many of us feel very angry and upset.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my constituency, many senior citizens complained to me that they were almost knocked down by PMDs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These riders are ubiquitous, in the corridors and void decks of HDB flats, department stores, food courts and even community centres and subway stations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the hawker centres in my area, there are often PMD riders going through and around.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of them are young people and ride very fast.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The situation is very bad, even the stall owners complained to me.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If someone tries to dissuade them, some riders will become fierce in their reaction.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For them, it is a given that pedestrians should always give way to them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, our pedestrians no longer feel safe in sharing walkways.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The old folks tell me that when they walk, they always feel very nervous, and they take every step with great apprehension.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some older people also asked me why the Government is promoting the use of PMDs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is this not going against our healthy lifestyle movement?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I ask the Government to re-examine the role of PMDs, taking into account national health care and future disease burdens.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Sir, I would like to propose that we strengthen enforcement on the ground substantially.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The lack of enforcement relative to the number of PMD users is a weak link and must be addressed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Repeat offenders must be banned from using such devices and we must have effective ways of ensuring that they comply with such bans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The AMA is an important piece of legislation that has allowed our society to take another positive step towards achieving the vision of a car-lite Singapore, with a sustainable public transportation system that is affordable, convenient and efficient for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: PMDs, PABs and bicycles have enabled Singaporeans, young and old, to get around with ease, improving first- and last-mile connectivity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The little to no emissions also lead to a cleaner and healthier living environment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, pedestrians, cyclists and users of PMDs and PABs with differing needs are now using public paths that were predominantly used by pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is, therefore, critical that a good balance is struck between the diverse needs of the various users.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The AMA paved some way towards regulating the conduct of the different users of the public paths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, months after the enactment of the Act, there is still much buzz on the ground about the issues faced by various path users.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This proposed Bill, which brings with it more specific legislation, is, therefore, important.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that starting with e-scooters, such process ensures that the devices are safe before they are used on the public path system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
