text: This allows for some monitoring of the mobility devices and vehicles that populate our paths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These inspections may be useful to ensure continued compliance with the regulations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are also proposed amendments to sections 30-34 of the Act to extend the scope of the ban on display, requirement to issue warning notices, advertisement and sale of non-compliant devices and vehicles.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that during the last debate in this House before the Active Mobility Bill was passed, there were some discussions regarding online sales and the challenges of enforcing these provisions on those sales.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note the Ministry’s position during the debate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also note that this legislation relates to conduct in the course of business and does not currently seem to cover individuals who advertise their products through social media or through platforms like Carousell.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There were also some discussions previously on compulsory insurance for riders of mobility devices or vehicles.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that if PMDs and mobility vehicles are here to stay, we may want to reconsider setting up requirements for compulsory insurance by the owners and riders.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: When such accidents take place, they inadvertently result in injuries and property damage.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, currently, the riders and users of PMDs or mobility vehicles are unlikely to be insured.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: If they are found to be personally liable for the damages and do not have funds to cover payment for compensation or injuries and damages, the injured pedestrian may be left out in the cold.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Compulsory insurance is, therefore, protection for both the rider and the injured pedestrian.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In any case, it would be prudent, as part of the education, for PMD users to be informed of insurance available.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Active mobility is a lifestyle choice and it must be supported by a culture of graciousness and considerate behaviour on the part of all users of public paths.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: All path users, be it the cyclists, PMD or PAB users or pedestrians, have a part to play to create a safe mobility culture in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note that there had been some grouses on the ground from riders regarding the rules on modification and speed limits.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe there would be continued efforts in educating the public about the need to be safe on the public paths so that they may appreciate the importance of these pieces of legislation and work together to build a positive culture within our community.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are currently two major groups of PMD users – the leisure users and the people who need them as a tool for their daily work.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Most commonly seen on the streets are food delivery persons.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The feedback I have heard from my residents is that it is often the food delivery riders who speed and ride more recklessly.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It might be because they are remunerated on a per-trip basis.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I would, therefore, like to suggest that the food delivery service providers also play their part in taking responsibilities towards the riding culture of their representatives.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Delivery service providers should also take charge of their riders and incentivise or penalise them according to their track records.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is the basic right of everyone to feel safe on our footpaths.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Every injury or fatality caused by PMDs is unnecessary and avoidable.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I, therefore, support measures to enhance enforcement capabilities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Of course, we ideally hope to live in a society where everyone is a considerate and gracious road and path user.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The mattress caught fire from the battery which was being charged.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Fortunately, the residents were home and put out the fire and no one was injured.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: On the ground, we have been advising residents not to overcharge devices or leave them charging overnight.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to do more to educate good safety and user habits.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to ensure a safe and harmonious sharing of public amenities, such as roads and pathways, for our people.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to seek some clarifications, and I have some suggestions for the Ministry to consider.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, Mr Speaker, I broadly agree with the intent of outsourcing enforcement actions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The new laws can only be effective if they are supported by sustained enforcement actions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The outsourced enforcement officers can be an important supplementary force when it comes to enforcement, as it would not be prudent for LTA to employ hundreds more enforcement officers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, therefore, important that these officers be adequately trained as an authorised representative of LTA as they represent Government authority when carrying out their duties.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under section 11(1)(d) of the proposed amendments to the LTA Act, Outsourced Enforcement Officers “must have suitable qualifications or experience”.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What lessons has LTA learnt from the programme?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am of the view that Volunteer Wardens and the Outsourced Enforcement Officers can and should complement each other in keeping our shared pathways safe for all users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: That said, will LTA also consider using technology to reduce the reliance on manpower for enforcement?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, having a common fleet management system to track and monitor the use of all active mobility devices could better aid in the deployment of the limited ground resources.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Videos of PMDs speeding across crossings, even when the traffic lights were not in their favour, have been widely circulated on social media.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, if the proposed measure to stop and look out for vehicles at road crossings fails to yield a reduction in the number of accidents at such road crossings, would the Ministry consider introducing rules to mandate dismounting the PMD at road and zebra crossings?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Much like how we would be required to pass a test before being allowed to drive a motor vehicle, would LTA consider making training mandatory for PMD users?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For a start, to minimise cost and administrative work, training could be conducted online, with users taking a quiz to ensure that they have sufficient safety knowledge prior to registration and riding of a PMD.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Alternatively, introducing signs, such as “stop and look out for oncoming traffic” at suitable road crossings could potentially help in reminding PMD users to take ownership to ride safely and work towards the safe sharing of pathways for the people around them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some of the pedestrians involved in these accidents had suffered very serious injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This begs the question whether third-party liability insurance should be made mandatory for PMD users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The virtue of mandatory insurance would ensure that victims would get a justified amount of compensation and the offending PMD users would not escape the consequences of their action.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Adopting a similar liability and compensation framework as per motor vehicles could go a long way in ensuring that the victims would not be overly burdened by medical expenses in the event of a serious accident.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the overall active mobility ecosystem, PMD retailers play a crucial role as a gatekeeper of compliant models into the market.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Section 32 of AMA acknowledges this, and the Bill makes further refinements on what the retailer can advertise.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the regulations seem to place the emphasis solely on physical brick-and-mortar retail shops which, presumably, are easier to enforce against.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But what about online retailers selling non-compliant devices?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some weeks back, The Straits Times featured a story about an online seller operating out of an HDB flat in Yishun and he had more than 40 e-scooters stocked up in the 4-room HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the article, a buyer commented that his e-scooter battery bought from this online retailer became faulty after just 10 days, while a neighbour was worried about the possibility of a fire breaking out in this "home warehouse".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Motorised wheelchairs are meant for use by the disabled and the elderly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These motorised wheelchairs can be costly to purchase, particularly for those with severe conditions and have financial constraints.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Expanding the AMA to govern these motorised wheelchairs could, therefore, have a negative impact on the most disadvantaged within our society.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, this sum can be minor, especially if charged against big companies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Where possible, we should embrace smart enforcement and reduce our reliance on manpower.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Several Members of the House have emphasised the importance of safety on public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: When the Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP) released its recommendations on measures to enhance path safety in end-August and when the Government announced our acceptance of the recommendations in early September, we similarly heard many comments about path safety, with some members of the public advocating for PMDs to be completely banned from public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It provides more first- and last-mile options and complements the more traditional modes of transport.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Active mobility devices provide new mobility options to those with walking difficulties and relatively cheap and convenient options for commuting or even for the purpose of work.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Many Members of the House, including Mr Zainal Sapari, Mr Louis Ng and Ms Rahayu Mahzam, have acknowledged these benefits.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Rather than banning these devices, we should strike a balance to allow us to harness the potential of active mobility while mitigating the disamenities.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have, therefore, put in place a system of rules and regulations to govern the usage of devices on public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Each measure should not be seen in isolation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also complement these with strict enforcement efforts, widespread education measures and infrastructural improvements where we can.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Mr Zainal Sapari, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Melvin Yong called for third-party liability insurance to be made mandatory.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: AMAP had considered the impact of this on the diverse group of active mobility users and determined that it was ultimately more important to prevent accidents from happening in the first place.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We agree with the Panel and will instead strengthen regulations to safeguard the safety of path users.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With regard to Ms Rahayu Mahzam's suggestion of tapping on the Small Claims Tribunal for personal injury claims up to $20,000, we understand that the Tribunal does not hear personal injury claims.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Instead, we have accepted the Panel's recommendation to raise awareness of, and accessibility to, existing avenues of seeking compensation, such as working with the Singapore Mediation Centre on making mediation more readily accessible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Mr Ang Hin Kee and Miss Cheng Li Hui have suggested, we will continue to strongly encourage and promote the take-up of third-party liability insurance, focusing on large employers of active mobility device users, such as food delivery companies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Some companies, such as Deliveroo, already provide insurance for their riders and we encourage all other companies to do so as well.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui pointed out that food delivery companies also need to play their part to ensure their riders ride safely.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is part of their duty under the Workplace Safety and Health Act.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The Ministry of Manpower, LTA and the Traffic Police have issued a joint circular to delivery companies with concrete suggestions of steps they can take.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Delivery companies should monitor the riding behaviour of their riders, for instance, by providing an avenue for public reporting, and also train and educate their riders on the active mobility regulations and safe riding behaviours.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Joan Pereira also spoke about increasing penalties for riders who cause serious injury to victims.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Those who cause grievous hurt can face even higher penalties under the Penal Code.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In the case of a rider riding rashly, he can face up to $10,000 in fines and up to four years' imprisonment.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To answer Mr Dennis Tan's query, the criminal justice system has different mechanisms for dealing with offenders who are under the age of 21.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: While these issues lie outside the scope of this Bill, I assure Members that we work closely with AMAP to continually review our active mobility rules and regulations, and we will take these suggestions into account when discussing the key areas of review with AMAP.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I would also like to reassure Mr Melvin Yong that we will certainly monitor the situation after AMAP's recommendations are implemented, and review the measures as necessary, depending on the prevailing situation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA's team of 50 Active Mobility Enforcement Officers (AMEOs) have issued over 3,000 advisories for unsafe riding on paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The measures in this Bill, including the PMD registration regime and the empowerment of outsourced enforcement officers, will further strengthen our enforcement efforts.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA is conducting a trial to study the effectiveness of mobile closed-circuit televisions (CCTVs) in identifying and reducing errant riding behaviours along public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to explore how technology can enhance and complement our enforcement efforts, so as to allow us to be effective while being manpower-lean.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We enforce strictly against retailers in Singapore that sell non-compliant devices for use on public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We also wish to inform Ms Thanaletchimi that LTA can require retailers to display notices about the different types of devices and the relevant device criteria at their premises.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To address Mr Dennis Tan's concern, members of the public are encouraged to report retailers who willfully misrepresent the device specifications to LTA and we will not hesitate to take firm action against such retailers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Melvin Yong have asked about online retailers of PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Where feasible, LTA engages online marketplace operators to remove postings of non-compliant devices, most of which are agreeable to doing so.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, some online retailers are based overseas which limits our ability to enforce against them.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ultimately, PMD users must also exercise caution and take personal responsibility in choosing the device to buy and ride on public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is in the consumers' interest to check that the devices they buy comply with the device criteria.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to monitor the situation, including studying Mr Ang Hin Kee and Mr Dennis Tan's suggestions to raise public awareness of the legitimate retailers who sell compliant devices and of the popular device models which comply with our device criteria.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Mr Ang Hin Kee, Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Ms Rahayu Mahzam have highlighted, educational efforts are important to cultivate a culture of safe and gracious path sharing.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We have rolled out several public education outreach initiatives along with the Safe Riding Programme (SRP) for active mobility users.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As I earlier mentioned, over 9,000 riders have gone through SRP since it was launched in February this year.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Delivery riders, such as those from Deliveroo, have also attended the programme.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We encourage all active mobility device users to attend the SRP to learn and practise safe riding behaviours.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: It is probably not necessary at the moment to have mandatory training, but we will certainly expand our outreach and engagement efforts to all members of the public.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Our active mobility infrastructure also helps to safeguard the safety of path users.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the width of footpaths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Apart from this, we are building dedicated cycling infrastructure where possible and introducing pedestrian priority zones (PPZ) at locations along cycling paths with potentially high pedestrian-cyclist interactions.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will continue to improve our infrastructure island-wide, but these will take time to implement.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I would also like to thank Er Dr Lee Bee Wah for the clarification on an example of disallowing the use of PMDs in Town Council areas.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I would be happy to get more details from her on the case and advise her accordingly.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: But it will be sufficient for me to remind Members of the House that the AMA serves to ensure that all public paths are made available for the use of active mobility users, and that rules are applied consistently so that users will not be confused with different rules at different areas.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I hope I have addressed the Members' concerns about active mobility safety.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As with the introduction of any new mode of transport, it will take time for all user groups to adjust.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As Mr Ang Hin Kee and Mr Louis Ng pointed out, ultimately, the key is for Singapore to develop a safe and gracious sharing culture for our public paths, where everyone plays a part in keeping our paths safe.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I will now move on to address the Members' questions on the Bill.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: As mentioned earlier, applicants will have to declare that their device is compliant with the device criteria upon registration.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam had suggested undertaking measures to ensure continued compliance with the device criteria.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will consider appropriate measures and will continue to enforce against non-compliant devices found on public paths.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Louis Ng asked about the parties that can register PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will take into account Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Thanaletchimi's feedback when deciding on the age for individuals who wish to register PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether LTA can refuse to register PMDs for individuals who were previously convicted of active mobility-related offences.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, prohibiting the individual from registering a PMD does not prevent them from riding PMDs that they rent or borrow.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the circumstances in which PMDs can be deregistered.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We expect the bulk of deregistrations to be due to applications by the registrant, and LTA deregistering non-compliant PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Legislatively, we have also provided for deregistration if LTA is satisfied that the device has ceased to be used on any footpath or shared path, and if the device is wholly unfit for further use.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is intended to cover scenarios like a deceased person's next-of-kin applying to deregister a PMD with sufficient proof of disposal, or when the PMD has deteriorated and is no longer serviceable.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Louis Ng asked how registrants should deal with changes of ownership or when their PMDs cease to be used.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If the registrant has sold his PMD to another person, he should apply to LTA to transfer the registration to the buyer.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If the registrant has ceased to use the PMD, there is currently no legal obligation for him to deregister the PMD.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: However, it is in his interest to do so as he would otherwise continue to be held responsible for the PMD.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will facilitate this by reminding registrants to deregister their devices if they are no longer being used.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Owners should also ensure that their PMDs are properly disposed of to prevent subsequent misuse.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This will ensure that they do not face the situation of continuing liability that Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Louis Ng highlighted.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked how the 10 km/h device speed limit will impact genuine users of PMAs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is why AMAP has consulted agencies involved in eldercare and with the disability community.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We understand that occupational therapists do not generally recommend devices that travel above 10 km/h for the patients' own safety.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: AMAP also found that the vast majority of PMAs available in the market today already comply with this device speed limit.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Thus, genuine users of PMAs should have little difficulty in complying with the new criterion.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For those users who may require more assistance to comply, we will explore what we can do to assist them.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Miss Cheng Li Hui and Mr Melvin Yong expressed concern about fires caused by motorised PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I would also like to clarify with Mr Gan Thiam Poh that this is a separate initiative from the e-scooter registration regime.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Devices will be certified according to UL's testing requirements.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I have earlier mentioned the explicit authorisation that they will have to receive from the Chief Executive of LTA on the powers they can exercise.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: They have to be in uniform and display their identification card.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To address Ms Thanaletchimi’s concern, uniforms will make the OEOs more recognisable to the general public.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will also undertake publicity measures to ensure the public is aware of the powers conferred on the OEOs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: To answer Mr Louis Ng’s question, OEOs are subject to broader checks and balances when exercising their statutory powers, including possible judicial review, as are other enforcement officers, such as the Police and LTA officers.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked about the qualifications and training of OEOs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Suitable qualifications include the private security guard licence as well as relevant security industry certifications, such as Workforce Skills Qualifications (WSQ).

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: LTA will also ensure that the OEOs are suitably trained and have the necessary skillsets to carry out their functions safely and efficiently.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I would also like to clarify with Mr Louis Ng that the amendment to section 50 of the AMA provides OEOs with the power to seize vehicles which are connected with offences under the AMA, such as non-compliant PMDs.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: OEOs will not be granted powers of disposal under the AMA.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked why the Bill removes the need for LTA to locate the owner prior to disposing of a vehicle under section 53 of the AMA.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: This is because section 50 of the AMA already requires LTA to notify the owner, if known, of the seizure.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked whether the proposed penalties for causing damage to road infrastructure are sufficient to deter companies.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: In summary, this Bill supports our vision for a better and safer transport system by enhancing LTA's enforcement and regulatory powers.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Just now, the Senior Minister of State talked about compensation via mediation and this is provided that both parties agree to attend the mediation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: My question is: what if one party refuses to attend the mediation or the end result of mediation is not satisfactory?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: What recourse does the injured party have, besides taking legal action?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: My second question is: Nee Soon Town Council has our by-laws where no cycling is allowed in open spaces and common areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: Can this continue to be implemented under the new AMA or otherwise?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The one which Er Dr Lee Bee Wah mentioned was through a private settlement via mediation.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Of course, if the parties can reach an agreement, such an agreement can be enforced via a contract.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The other possible avenue where victims can seek compensation is through civil action, that is, to pursue a civil claim.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: For this, the victim may have to initiate legal proceedings against the cyclist or the person who caused the injury.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And if the Court rules in favour of the victim, then the Court will order the defendant to pay damages to the plaintiff.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The last modality where victims can seek redress is to file a Police report of the incident and the Police will then carry out investigations to establish the cause and liability and, depending on the outcome of the investigation, the offender may be charged for offences like speeding or reckless riding under the AMA or for causing grievous hurt to others by a rash act under the Penal Code.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: If the offender is found guilty, then the Court may also decide on the compensation amount that the injured person will receive.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: The only exception to this are void decks.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Void decks are excluded from AMA because they are not critical for connectivity and the safety concerns at void decks are also stronger because of the layout, such as pillars.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: And for this, Town Councils can choose to enact their own by-laws relating to the use of active mobility devices in void decks.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Like I have said, LTA will be happy to find out the details from Er Dr Lee Bee Wah on the incident or the example that she brought up, and we will work with the Town Council to see how we can better address some of the safety concerns in those areas mentioned by the Member.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yes, there is such a right to commence action in Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if the injuries are not very serious, the legal cost of commencing such an action may not be very worthwhile for parties to commence action in Court.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, in effect, for many people who suffered injuries which are not very serious in such incidents, the right of recourse to the Courts may well be just an academic one.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: Other than those avenues that I have mentioned, most importantly, we need to educate road users, path users as well as PMD users on the right etiquette to ride responsibly and safely.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: With that, we hope that such incidents or accidents can be minimised.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: It could be between two coffee shops or between two supermarkets.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: LTA should give Town Councils more leeway to manage the Town Council areas.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: They know which are the areas that are dangerous and which are the areas that have high pedestrian traffic.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I hope that LTA can amend the AMA in this aspect so that the residents are safe at all times.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I have also mentioned that we will work with the Member to see how we can address some of these concerns.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: There can be other mitigating measures like making those vulnerable areas Pedestrian Priority Zones (PPZ) so that PMD users will exercise due diligence and caution when approaching such places and also, for road users or pathway users, to exercise caution as well to prevent potential incidents from happening.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: I take it that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah is very passionate about this issue and that she is very concerned about the safety of her residents and so are we, and we will work with her to see how we can best address these concerns.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: Even with the best education, it only requires one irresponsible PMD user to cause an accident.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: If let us, say, the amount of compensation is huge, even after taking a legal recourse, the PMD users might not be able to pay that kind of compensation due to financial difficulty.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: What recourse then would the accident victims have in such a situation?

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We will work with the General Insurance Association as well as insurance companies to explore ways to make third-party insurance more affordable and more accessible.

speaker: Dr Lam Pin Min
text: We are also considering whether we can include the option of bundling third-party liability insurance into the sale of the PMDs so that when PMD users purchase their PMDs, it comes with third-party liability insurance as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.20 pm until 4.40 pm.
